Over the next 6 months, follow-up imaging noted continued nonunion and increased right-sided displacement (Figure 1). The patient was seen for a second opinion because of his continued pain and torticollis and was subsequently offered surgical intervention. The patient was admitted the day before surgery and placed in 15 pounds of cervical traction with the goal of attaining improved alignment before surgery. On the day of surgery, anesthesia was induced and video-assisted laryngoscopy was used to attain endo

have resulted in right-sided stretch and contralateral compression during the correction perioperatively. In addition, there was considerable cranial settling and posterior displacement of the occiput noted both in the preoperative and postoperative imaging (Figures 1, E and 2, D). This displacement likely led to compression and stretching of the nerve, which would have placed the nerve at a significantly higher risk of injury. The original injury and subsequent displacement could also be an explanation for the temporary palsy the patient had experienced postoperatively after his C3-T4 fusion.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Preoperative anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the cervical spine, showing findings consistent with Jefferson fracture in the context of a case report. B: Cervical spine MRI demonstrating complete transverse atlantal ligament (TAL) rupture and mild cervical intervertebral disk protrusion, which are critical findings in this presentation of Jefferson fracture. C: CT imaging reveals specific bony pathology of the atlas, including lateral mass displacement and fractures of both anterior and posterior arches, characteristic of Jefferson fracture and associated dislocation.

panels.figure_caption: Preoperative imaging findings: (A) Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the cervical spine. (B) Cervical spine MRI demonstrating complete transverse atlantal ligament (TAL) rupture (yellow circle), mild cervical intervertebral disk protrusion, and no spinal cord compression. (C) Cervical spine CT showing a displaced fracture at the transitional region between the right anterior arch and lateral mass of the atlas combined with atlantoaxial dislocation (red arrow), as well as a fracture of the left posterior arch (yellow arrow).
in_text_mentions: Cervical X-ray (open-mouth projection) demonstrated asymmetric atlantodental intervals along with degenerative alterations in the cervical spine. CT imaging revealed a displaced fracture at the transitional zone between the right anterior arch and lateral mass of the atlas with concomitant atlantoaxial dislocation, along with a left posterior arch fracture. MRI showed complete rupture of the transverse atlantal ligament (TAL), mild cervical disk protrusion, and no evidence of spinal cord compression (Figure 1).

After advanced trauma life support (ATLS) was applied to the patient and stabilized, a thorough history and detailed physical examination were obtained. He complained of neck and right arm pain. The pain was localized to the neck and right arm without any radiation. No history of head trauma or loss of consciousness was reported. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: CT shows avulsion fracture of the right transverse atlantal ligament, a component of Jefferson fracture. B: CT shows bilateral posterior arch fractures of the atlas, characteristic of Jefferson fracture. C: CT shows displacement of the C1 lateral mass, indicating fracture involvement. D: CT shows enlargement of the Atlantodental Interval (ADI), suggesting malalignment associated with Jefferson fracture. E: T2 MRI shows high signal intensity in avulsed osseous tubercle and fractured arch, consistent with acute ligament/bone injury. F: T2 MRI reveals edema and hemorrhagic changes in surrounding ligaments and disc, consistent with severe acute trauma/Jefferson fracture.

Fortunately, he had no neurological deficits in either the spinal cord or cranial nerves.
